questions.stem: How is DNA packaged in the nucleus of a human cell?
options: Coated in phospholipid to form many small vesicles
Wound around histone proteins to form chromosomes
As small free circles floating in the nucleoplasm
Attached to ribosomes on the nuclear membrane
questions.explanation: Nuclear DNA is wrapped around histone proteins and coiled to form chromatin, which condenses into visible chromosomes before cell division. Free circular DNA is found in mitochondria.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares nuclear DNA and mitochondrial DNA in humans?
options: Both are linear and bound to histone proteins in the same way
Both are circular, but only mitochondrial DNA codes for proteins
Nuclear DNA is linear and bound to proteins; mitochondrial DNA is circular and unbound
Nuclear DNA is circular and unbound; mitochondrial DNA is linear and bound to proteins
questions.explanation: Nuclear DNA forms long linear molecules bound to histones in 46 chromosomes. Mitochondrial DNA is a small circular molecule, not bound to histones, carrying a few genes needed by the mitochondrion.

questions.stem: A man and a woman have a son. From whom does the son inherit his mitochondrial DNA, and why?
options: Equally from both parents, as with the chromosomes in the nucleus
From his father only, because he inherits his father's Y chromosome
From his mother, because mitochondria in the zygote come from the egg
From his father, because the sperm's midpiece is packed with mitochondria
questions.explanation: The zygote's mitochondria come from the egg's cytoplasm; sperm mitochondria are not passed on. Mitochondrial DNA is therefore inherited through the maternal line by both sons and daughters.

questions.stem: What information does a gene carry?
options: The pattern of sugars that forms the DNA backbone
The code for the order of amino acids in a polypeptide
The code for the sequence of fatty acids in a lipid
The instructions for the number of chromosomes in a cell
questions.explanation: A gene is a section of DNA whose base sequence codes for the amino acid sequence of a polypeptide or protein. Proteins then determine the structure and function of cells.

questions.stem: How does DNA determine the structure and function of a cell?
options: It leaves the nucleus and becomes part of the cell membrane and organelles
It is broken down to release energy that powers all of the cell's activities
It directly forms the cytoskeleton that gives the cell its shape
It codes for the proteins, such as enzymes, that the cell makes
questions.explanation: DNA codes for proteins: enzymes control the cell's reactions and structural proteins form its parts, so the proteins made determine what the cell is like and what it does. DNA itself stays in the nucleus.

questions.stem: DNA is a polymer of nucleotides. What is each DNA nucleotide made of?
options: A fatty acid, deoxyribose sugar and a nitrogenous base
An amino group, glucose and a phosphate group
A phosphate, deoxyribose sugar and a nitrogenous base
A phosphate group, ribose sugar and an amino acid
questions.explanation: Each DNA nucleotide has a phosphate, the sugar deoxyribose and one of four bases (A, T, G or C). Ribose is the sugar in RNA.

questions.stem: Which bases pair together in DNA?
options: Adenine with uracil; guanine with cytosine
Adenine with thymine; guanine with cytosine
Adenine with guanine; thymine with cytosine
Adenine with cytosine; guanine with thymine
questions.explanation: Complementary base pairing always joins A to T and G to C. Uracil replaces thymine only in RNA.

questions.stem: A sample of human DNA contains 30% adenine. What percentage of its bases are guanine?
questions.explanation: Adenine pairs with thymine, so T is also 30%, making 60% A and T together. The remaining 40% is shared equally between G and C, giving 20% guanine.

questions.stem: What holds the two strands of the DNA double helix together?
options: Weak hydrogen bonds between complementary bases
Strong covalent bonds between the phosphate groups
Peptide bonds between neighbouring sugar molecules
Ionic bonds between the histones and the bases
questions.explanation: Hydrogen bonds between base pairs are individually weak, so the strands can be separated for replication and transcription. Strong covalent bonds link nucleotides along each strand's sugar-phosphate backbone.

questions.stem: Why is it important that the bonds between base pairs are weak while the bonds along each strand are strong?
options: The base sequence can be rearranged during copying to produce useful variation
The molecule can be broken into single nucleotides that are respired for energy
The two strands can be swapped between chromosomes each time the cell divides
The strands can separate for copying while each strand keeps its base sequence
questions.explanation: Weak hydrogen bonds let helicase unzip the helix, while the strong backbone keeps each strand's sequence intact to serve as a template. This combination allows accurate replication.

questions.stem: DNA replication is semi-conservative. What does this term mean?
options: Each new molecule is made of fragments of old and new DNA mixed along both strands
Only half of the genes on each chromosome are copied in each cell cycle
Each new DNA molecule has one original strand and one newly made strand
Half of the original DNA molecules are kept and half are broken down
questions.explanation: Each original strand acts as a template for a new complementary strand, so every daughter molecule keeps one parental strand. Fragments mixed along both strands would be a dispersive model, which experiments ruled out.

questions.stem: What is the role of DNA polymerase in replication?
options: Copying the DNA base sequence into a molecule of messenger RNA
Adding nucleotides to build a new strand complementary to the template
Unwinding the double helix by breaking the hydrogen bonds between bases
Joining amino acids together in the order coded by the DNA
questions.explanation: DNA polymerase adds nucleotides that pair with the exposed template bases, building the new strand. Unwinding is carried out by helicase, and copying DNA into mRNA is transcription by RNA polymerase.

questions.stem: A template DNA strand reads 3' TACGGT 5'. What is the sequence of the new strand made during replication?
options: 5' AUGCCA 3'
5' TACGGT 3'
5' ATGCCA 3'
5' UACGGU 3'
questions.explanation: DNA polymerase adds nucleotides complementary to the template: T pairs with A, A with T, C with G and G with C. A new DNA strand contains thymine, not uracil.

questions.stem: Where do transcription and translation take place in a human cell?
options: Both in the nucleus, before the protein leaves the cell
Both at ribosomes on the rough endoplasmic reticulum
Transcription in the nucleus; translation at ribosomes
Transcription at ribosomes; translation in the nucleus
questions.explanation: A gene is transcribed into mRNA in the nucleus; the mRNA leaves through nuclear pores and is translated into a polypeptide at a ribosome. DNA itself never leaves the nucleus.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares DNA and messenger RNA?
options: Both contain thymine, but only DNA leaves the nucleus
DNA is double-stranded with thymine; mRNA is single-stranded with uracil
DNA is single-stranded with uracil; mRNA is double-stranded with thymine
Both are double-stranded, but only mRNA contains deoxyribose
questions.explanation: mRNA is a single strand containing ribose and uracil in place of thymine. Its job is to carry the gene's code out of the nucleus, which DNA does not do.

questions.stem: A section of the DNA template strand reads TAC GGA. Which mRNA sequence is transcribed from it?
options: TAC GGA
AUG CCU
ATG CCT
UAC GGA
questions.explanation: RNA polymerase builds mRNA complementary to the template, with uracil pairing with adenine: T to A, A to U, C to G and G to C. A sequence containing T could not be RNA.

questions.stem: What is a codon?
options: A complete gene that codes for one finished polypeptide chain
Three mRNA bases that code for one amino acid or a stop signal
A sequence of three tRNA bases that pairs with the bases of the DNA template
A single base on DNA that codes for the position of one amino acid
questions.explanation: The genetic code is read in triplets on mRNA called codons. The complementary triplet on a tRNA molecule is an anticodon.

questions.stem: What is the role of transfer RNA (tRNA) in translation?
options: It carries the gene's code from the nucleus out to the ribosome
It forms the structure of the ribosome and joins amino acids together
It unwinds the DNA so that the gene can be read by RNA polymerase
It carries an amino acid and pairs its anticodon with an mRNA codon
questions.explanation: Each tRNA carries one kind of amino acid; its anticodon binds the matching codon so amino acids are placed in the coded order. Carrying the code out of the nucleus is the role of mRNA.

questions.stem: An mRNA codon reads GCU. What is the anticodon on the tRNA that pairs with it?
options: GCU
CGT
GCA
CGA
questions.explanation: The anticodon is complementary to the codon: G pairs with C, C with G and U with A, giving CGA. tRNA contains uracil, not thymine.

questions.stem: A section of mRNA contains 300 bases from the start codon up to, but not including, the stop codon. How many amino acids does it code for?
questions.explanation: Each amino acid is coded by a three-base codon, so 300 / 3 = 100 codons and 100 amino acids. The stop codon codes for no amino acid and was excluded.

questions.stem: What happens when the ribosome reaches a stop codon on the mRNA?
options: The mRNA is copied back into DNA to make another gene
The ribosome reverses and translates the mRNA backwards
Translation ends and the completed polypeptide is released
A final amino acid is added that seals the end of the chain
questions.explanation: Stop codons code for no amino acid and have no matching tRNA; release factors end translation and free the polypeptide. The start codon AUG, by contrast, codes for methionine.

questions.stem: Several different codons can code for the same amino acid. What is one consequence of this?
options: Every change to a single base changes the protein's whole sequence
Each gene can be translated into several completely different proteins
The genetic code differs from one tissue type to another in the body
Some changes to a single base do not change the amino acid sequence
questions.explanation: Because the code is degenerate, a substitution in the third base of a codon often gives a codon for the same amino acid, so the protein is unchanged. The code is the same in all cells.

questions.stem: Which sequence of events describes protein synthesis?
options: DNA unwinds, mRNA is transcribed, mRNA moves to a ribosome, tRNA brings amino acids, peptide bonds form
mRNA unwinds, DNA is transcribed, DNA moves to a ribosome, tRNA brings amino acids, peptide bonds form
DNA unwinds, tRNA is transcribed, tRNA moves to the nucleus, mRNA brings amino acids, peptide bonds form
DNA moves to a ribosome, amino acids attach to DNA, mRNA joins the amino acids, the protein is released
questions.explanation: The gene is transcribed into mRNA in the nucleus, and at the ribosome tRNA molecules deliver amino acids that are joined by peptide bonds in the order set by the codons. DNA does not leave the nucleus.

questions.stem: Before leaving the nucleus, a newly made pre-mRNA has sections called introns removed. What is the result?
options: The DNA of the gene loses its introns so it is shorter next time
The mRNA becomes double-stranded so it is protected in the cytoplasm
The mature mRNA carries only the coding exons to the ribosome
The mature mRNA carries only the non-coding sections to the ribosome
questions.explanation: Splicing removes introns and joins the exons, the parts that code for amino acids. The DNA of the gene is unchanged; only the RNA copy is edited.

questions.stem: What does epigenetics study?
options: Changes in gene expression that do not involve changes to the DNA base sequence
Changes in the DNA base sequence caused by errors during DNA replication
The way genes are passed from parents to offspring by meiosis and fertilisation
The number and structure of chromosomes shown in a person's karyotype
questions.explanation: Epigenetics concerns how genes are switched on or off, for example by chemical tags on DNA or histones, without altering the sequence itself. Changes to the sequence are mutations.

questions.stem: How does adding methyl groups to a gene's DNA usually affect it?
options: It increases the rate at which the gene is replicated
It moves the gene from the nucleus to the mitochondria
It reduces transcription, so less of the protein is made
It changes the base sequence, so a different protein is made
questions.explanation: Methylation of DNA, especially near a gene's start, generally silences the gene by blocking transcription. The base sequence itself is not changed.

questions.stem: Identical twins have the same DNA sequence, yet differences in their gene expression increase as they age. What is the best explanation?
options: Their genes are lost from chromosomes at different rates as they get older
Different environments and lifestyles lead to different epigenetic marks on their DNA
Their DNA base sequences gradually become different through crossing over in body cells
One twin inherits more mitochondrial DNA than the other as they grow older
questions.explanation: Factors such as diet, smoking and stress alter DNA methylation and histone modification, so twins' patterns of gene expression drift apart. Crossing over occurs only in meiosis, not in body cells.

questions.stem: Histone proteins can be chemically modified so that the DNA wrapped around them is packed less tightly. What is the likely effect?
options: Genes in that region are permanently deleted from the chromosome
Genes in that region are copied into many extra versions of the gene
Genes in that region change their base sequence to a new allele
Genes in that region become easier to reach and transcribe
questions.explanation: Loosely packed chromatin lets RNA polymerase and other proteins reach the genes, increasing transcription; tightly packed chromatin keeps genes switched off. No sequence change is involved.

questions.stem: Every body cell in a person contains the same genes, yet a liver cell and a neuron make very different proteins. Why?
options: Each cell type contains a different set of chromosomes
Liver cells and neurons use different genetic codes
Neurons lose the genes they do not need during mitosis
Different genes are switched on in different cell types
questions.explanation: Cells differ because of which genes they express, controlled by transcription factors (products of other genes), epigenetic marks and signals from the environment. Their DNA is the same.

questions.stem: A study finds that people whose mothers experienced famine during pregnancy show different methylation of certain genes decades later. What does this suggest?
options: Methylation patterns are fixed at fertilisation and cannot be influenced by anything
Famine causes extra chromosomes to form, which increases methylation of the genes
The environment before birth can cause lasting epigenetic changes in gene expression
Famine changes the DNA base sequence of the foetus by causing mutations in every gene
questions.explanation: Studies of people exposed to famine before birth have linked prenatal conditions to altered DNA methylation in adulthood, showing that environment can have long-lasting effects on gene expression without changing the sequence.

questions.stem: What does the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) do?
options: Makes many copies of a specific section of DNA
Separates DNA fragments according to their size
Joins a human gene into a bacterial plasmid
Translates a gene into its protein outside a cell
questions.explanation: PCR uses cycles of heating and cooling with a heat-stable DNA polymerase to amplify a target DNA sequence many times. Separating fragments by size is gel electrophoresis.

questions.stem: In gel electrophoresis, why do DNA fragments move towards the positive electrode?
options: DNA is positively charged because of its nitrogenous bases
The gel pulls large fragments towards the positive end
The fragments are pushed along by the buffer solution's flow
DNA is negatively charged because of its phosphate groups
questions.explanation: Phosphate groups give DNA a negative charge, so it moves towards the positive electrode; smaller fragments move faster through the gel and travel further.

questions.stem: Sequencing the whole human genome showed that only a small percentage of the DNA codes for proteins. How has this changed understanding of DNA?
options: Scientists concluded that non-coding DNA is copied into proteins only in the mitochondria
Scientists concluded that most human genes are found on the Y chromosome
Scientists concluded that humans have far more genes than any other species
Research now also studies non-coding DNA, some of which regulates gene expression
questions.explanation: Finding that most of the genome does not code for proteins focused research on regulatory sequences and RNA that control gene expression. Humans do not have exceptionally many genes compared with other species.

questions.stem: DNA sequencing determines the order of bases in a section of DNA. How can this help understand an inherited disease?
options: Sequencing counts the person's chromosomes to see whether one is missing
Comparing sequences from affected and unaffected people can locate the mutation
Sequencing replaces the faulty gene in the patient's cells with a working copy
Sequencing measures how much protein a person's cells are producing at a given time
questions.explanation: Comparing base sequences shows exactly where a disease allele differs from the normal allele, revealing how the protein is changed. Replacing genes is gene therapy, and counting chromosomes is done with a karyotype.

questions.stem: What is the role of RNA polymerase in protein synthesis?
options: Joining amino acids with peptide bonds at the ribosome
Carrying amino acids from the cytoplasm to the ribosome
Joining fragments of new DNA together during replication
Building an mRNA strand complementary to the DNA template
questions.explanation: RNA polymerase binds to the start of a gene, separates the strands and assembles mRNA nucleotides complementary to the template strand. Peptide bonds form at the ribosome during translation.

questions.stem: During replication, one new strand is built in short fragments. Which enzyme joins these fragments into a continuous strand?
options: Helicase
RNA polymerase
Amylase
DNA ligase
questions.explanation: DNA polymerase can only build in one direction, so one strand is made in short sections that DNA ligase then joins together. Helicase unwinds the helix ahead of replication.

questions.stem: A single base change in a gene turns a codon for an amino acid into a stop codon near the start of the gene. What is the most likely effect on the protein?
options: One amino acid is swapped and the protein works almost normally
A longer polypeptide is made because translation continues past the end
A much shorter polypeptide is made that probably cannot function
The same protein is made, because the genetic code is degenerate
questions.explanation: A premature stop codon ends translation early, so the polypeptide is truncated and usually non-functional. Degeneracy only protects against changes that give another codon for the same amino acid.
